q: Which of the following is useful for testing univariate normality of distribution? (A) Q-Q plot (B) Shapiro-Wilk test (C) Jarque-Bera test (D) Scatter plot
who: Tests of univariate normality

concept.t: A Q-Q plot, the Shapiro-Wilk test and the Jarque-Bera test all check whether a single variable follows a normal distribution. A scatter plot needs two variables, so it cannot test univariate normality.

A Q-Q plot puts the data's quantiles against normal quantiles, and points on a straight line mean normality; Shapiro-Wilk compares ordered scores with expected normal scores, and Jarque-Bera tests whether skewness and kurtosis match a normal curve.
A significant Shapiro-Wilk or Jarque-Bera result (p below .05) means the data depart from normality. Scatter plots are used to check linearity and homoscedasticity between two variables.

wrong.1: Q-Q plot and Shapiro-Wilk are correct, but the list is incomplete: the Jarque-Bera test also tests univariate normality from skewness and kurtosis.
wrong.2: Shapiro-Wilk fits, but a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables, and the Q-Q plot and Jarque-Bera test are left out.
wrong.3: Wrongly includes the scatter plot, a bivariate graph for linearity, and leaves out the Jarque-Bera test, which checks skewness and kurtosis against the normal curve.

q: Which is the correct sequence of speech and language development according to Vygotsky? (A) Naive (B) Primitive (C) Egocentric (D) Ingrowth
who: Lev Vygotsky, Thought and Language (1934)

concept.t: Lev Vygotsky described four stages of speech: primitive (natural), naive psychology, egocentric speech and ingrowth. That is B, A, C, D.

(B) Primitive: crying, babbling and other pre-intellectual sounds; (A) Naive: words used correctly before their logic is grasped; (C) Egocentric: talking aloud to guide one's own actions; (D) Ingrowth: speech goes inward as silent inner speech.
For Vygotsky, egocentric speech does not simply die out, as Jean Piaget thought; it turns into inner speech that guides thinking.

wrong.1: Puts naive psychology before the primitive stage, but the primitive (natural) stage of crying and babbling is the starting point in Vygotsky's scheme.
wrong.3: Starts with naive instead of primitive and puts ingrowth before egocentric speech, when inner speech grows out of egocentric speech.
wrong.4: Gets the first two stages right but reverses the last two: egocentric speech comes first and only later turns inward as ingrowth (inner speech).

q: Match List I with List II. List I (Types of Reliability): (A) Test-retest (B) Alternate Form (delayed) (C) Coefficient alpha (D) Cohen's Kappa. List II (Source of Error Variance): (I) Content heterogeneity (II) Inter-scorer differences (III) Time sampling (IV) Content sampling and time sampling. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Anne Anastasi, sources of error variance in reliability

concept.t: Each reliability method picks up a different source of error: test-retest catches time sampling, delayed alternate forms catch content and time sampling, alpha catches content heterogeneity, and Cohen's kappa catches inter-scorer differences.

(A) Test-retest = (III) Time sampling; (B) Alternate form (delayed) = (IV) Content sampling and time sampling; (C) Coefficient alpha = (I) Content heterogeneity; (D) Cohen's kappa = (II) Inter-scorer differences.
Delayed alternate forms change both the items and the occasion, so two errors enter. Cohen's kappa measures agreement between two raters beyond chance, so its error is scorer disagreement.

wrong.1: Gives test-retest the double error of delayed alternate forms and pairs Cohen's kappa with time sampling; kappa is about agreement between raters, not occasions.
wrong.2: Uses time sampling twice, for alpha and kappa; coefficient alpha reflects item heterogeneity and kappa reflects inter-scorer differences.
wrong.4: Gets A and B right but swaps C and D: coefficient alpha reflects content heterogeneity, while inter-scorer differences belong to Cohen's kappa.

q: Which of the following are involved in decreased food intake and weight loss? (A) Insulin (B) Leptin (C) Cholecystokinin (D) Orexin
who: Satiety signals: leptin, insulin, cholecystokinin

concept.t: Leptin, insulin and cholecystokinin (CCK) all act as satiety signals that lower food intake. Orexin does the opposite: it increases hunger and eating.

Leptin from fat cells and insulin from the pancreas tell the hypothalamus how much fat the body stores, so high levels cut long-term intake. CCK is released by the gut during a meal and ends the meal sooner.
Eating up: ghrelin, orexin, neuropeptide Y; eating down: leptin, insulin (in the brain), CCK. Leptin-deficient ob/ob mice become very obese.

wrong.1: Leaves out cholecystokinin, a gut hormone released during a meal that signals fullness and shortens the meal.
wrong.3: Includes orexin (hypocretin), a lateral hypothalamic peptide that increases food intake and wakefulness, and leaves out CCK, which reduces intake.
wrong.4: Leaves out insulin, which acts in the brain as a long-term satiety signal, and wrongly includes orexin, which stimulates eating.

q: Jensen put forward the 'Regression' argument to account for which of the following?
who: Arthur Jensen, regression to the mean argument

concept.t: Arthur Jensen used the regression argument in the debate on Black-White IQ differences in the USA, so it was meant to account for group differences in intelligence.

Children of very bright parents score closer to the average than their parents (regression to the mean). Jensen argued that children of high-IQ Black and White parents regress towards different group means, and took this as evidence for a partly genetic group difference.
Critics replied that regression towards different group means is expected whatever causes the gap, so it does not prove a genetic cause.

wrong.1: Rising IQ scores across generations is the Flynn effect, described by James Flynn; Jensen's regression argument dealt with differences between racial groups.
wrong.2: Changes within one generation, such as IQ gains with age or schooling, were not its target; the argument compared groups.
wrong.4: Too broad: Jensen did hold that genes matter, but the regression argument was used specifically to explain the gap between groups.

q: Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Happiness results from experiences of personal expressiveness (B) Happiness is self-realization, meaning the expression and fulfilment of inner potentials (C) Happiness reflects an individual's own judgement about the quality of his or her life (D) Happiness results from the fulfilment of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. List II: (I) Ryan & Deci (II) Diener (III) Aristotle (IV) Waterman. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Eudaimonic and hedonic views of well-being

concept.t: Alan Waterman linked happiness to personal expressiveness, Aristotle to self-realisation (eudaimonia), Ed Diener to one's own judgement of life, and Richard Ryan and Edward Deci to three basic needs.
(A) Personal expressiveness = (IV) Waterman; (B) Self-realisation = (III) Aristotle; (C) Own judgement of life quality = (II) Diener; (D) Autonomy, competence, relatedness = (I) Ryan and Deci.

Hedonic views stress pleasure and life satisfaction (Diener's subjective well-being); eudaimonic views stress living true to one's potential (Aristotle, Waterman, and Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory).

wrong.1: Gives self-realisation to Diener and the three basic needs to Waterman; the three needs come from Ryan and Deci's self-determination theory.
wrong.2: Gives personal expressiveness to Aristotle and life judgement to Ryan and Deci; judging one's own life quality is Diener's subjective well-being.
wrong.4: Gives personal expressiveness to Diener and the three needs to Aristotle; autonomy, competence and relatedness come from Ryan and Deci.

q: Match List I with List II. List I: (A) The theory that an individual's self-concept is derived partly from membership in a group (B) The theory that prejudice arises from a real conflict of interest between groups (C) The theory that all societies are organised in group hierarchies and sustained through discrimination (D) The most important social perspective in social psychology. List II: (I) Realistic group conflict theory (II) Social Dominance theory (III) Social Identity theory (IV) Interdependence theory. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: As printed no option fits the true pairs A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV; option 1 fits if I and III were swapped in copying, and option 2 (also two pairs right) is the runner-up.
who: Henri Tajfel, Muzafer Sherif, Jim Sidanius, Harold Kelley

concept.t: Option (1) gets C and D right and only swaps the labels of A and B, the likeliest copying slip. The descriptions themselves match four well-known intergroup theories.

(A) Self-concept from group membership = Social identity theory (Henri Tajfel, John Turner); (B) Real conflict of interest = Realistic group conflict theory (Muzafer Sherif); (C) Hierarchies kept by discrimination = Social dominance theory (Jim Sidanius, Felicia Pratto); (D) = Interdependence theory (John Thibaut, Harold Kelley).
Sherif's Robbers Cave study is the classic test of realistic conflict; Tajfel's minimal group studies show bias even without any real conflict.

wrong.2: Gets A and C right but gives real conflict of interest to interdependence theory, when it is realistic group conflict theory (Muzafer Sherif).
wrong.3: Gives the hierarchy description to social identity theory and real conflict to social dominance theory; only D is right.
wrong.4: Gives self-concept to social dominance theory and hierarchies to interdependence theory; self-concept from groups is Tajfel and Turner's social identity theory.

q: The enhancement of dominant responses is strongest when people think they are being evaluated. What is the correct sequence of this theory? (A) Evaluation apprehension (B) Well learned (C) Presence of others (D) Increased arousal (E) Social facilitation
doubt: The textbook chain is C, A, D, B, E (presence of others comes first), which no option prints; option 4 only swaps the first two steps, while option 1 wrongly starts with the well-learned response.
who: Nickolas Cottrell, evaluation apprehension; Robert Zajonc, drive theory

concept.t: Option (4) gets the core chain right: arousal boosts the dominant (well-learned) response, giving social facilitation. Strictly, the presence of others comes before evaluation apprehension.

(C) Presence of others → (A) evaluation apprehension (worry about being judged) → (D) increased arousal → (B) the well-learned, dominant response becomes more likely → (E) social facilitation on easy tasks.
Robert Zajonc said the mere presence of others raises arousal. Nickolas Cottrell added that the effect is strongest when the others can evaluate us; blindfolded onlookers produced little effect.

wrong.1: Starts with the well-learned response, but the dominant response is the result of arousal, near the end of the chain, not its trigger.
wrong.2: Lists only four steps, leaves out the presence of others, and starts with arousal, when arousal follows evaluation apprehension.
wrong.3: Puts the well-learned response before the presence of others and arousal; in the theory, arousal comes first and then strengthens the dominant response.

q: Which technique of studying the brain involves injecting the patient with radioactive glucose?
who: Positron emission tomography (PET)

concept.t: In a PET scan the patient receives radioactive glucose or a similar tracer. Busy brain areas use more glucose, so they show up as active on the scan.
Detectors pick up the positrons given off by the tracer and a computer builds a colour map of activity. PET shows brain function, not just structure.
Structure: CT, MRI. Function: PET, fMRI (blood oxygen, no injection), EEG (electrical activity).

wrong.1: EEG records the brain's electrical activity through electrodes on the scalp; nothing is injected.
wrong.2: MRI uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to image brain structure; no radioactive tracer is used.
wrong.4: CT combines many X-ray images taken from different angles to show brain structure, not glucose use.

q: Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: The NEO-PI-R does not have a response style scale. Reason R: NEO-PI-R developers argued that adjustment of social desirability leads to a reduction in validity. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
who: Paul Costa and Robert McCrae, NEO-PI-R

concept.t: True. The NEO-PI-R by Paul Costa and Robert McCrae has no lie, faking or social desirability scale, unlike the MMPI with its L, F and K scales.
True. Costa and McCrae argued that socially desirable answers often reflect real traits, so correcting scores for social desirability makes them less valid, not more.
They left a response style scale out of the test precisely because they believed such corrections lower validity.

wrong.2: R is not a side fact: it is the stated reason why the authors chose not to build a response style scale into the test.
wrong.3: R is true: Costa and McCrae did argue that adjusting scores for social desirability reduces validity.
wrong.4: A is true: the NEO-PI-R has no formal response style or validity scale like the MMPI's L, F and K.

q: Which of the following are comprised in executive functions? (A) Planning (B) Attention (C) Set shifting (D) Declarative memory
who: Executive functions of the prefrontal cortex

concept.t: Executive functions are the control processes that run goal-directed behaviour: planning, controlling attention and set shifting. Declarative memory is a memory store, not a control process.
They depend mainly on the prefrontal cortex. Common tests are the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (set shifting), Tower of London (planning) and Stroop (inhibition and attention).
Akira Miyake's model names three core executive functions: shifting, updating of working memory and inhibition.

wrong.2: Includes declarative memory, the conscious memory for facts and events that depends on the hippocampus, and leaves out set shifting, a core executive function.
wrong.3: Leaves out attention control and wrongly includes declarative memory, which is a long-term memory system, not an executive process.
wrong.4: Leaves out planning, a classic executive function, and includes declarative memory, which is stored knowledge rather than control.

q: Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: According to Classical Test Theory (CTT) total variance is equal to the sum of true variance and error variance. Reason R: Error variance and true variance are independent of each other as per CTT. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
who: Classical test theory, X = T + E

concept.t: True. In classical test theory an observed score is true score plus error (X = T + E), and total variance splits as σ2X = σ2T + σ2E.
True. CTT assumes error is random and uncorrelated with true scores.
The variance of a sum equals the sum of the variances plus twice their covariance. Because T and E are independent, the covariance is zero, so total variance is simply true plus error variance.

wrong.2: R is the very condition that makes A hold: without zero covariance between true and error scores, an extra covariance term would appear.
wrong.3: R is true: independence of true and error scores is a core assumption of classical test theory.
wrong.4: A is true: in classical test theory total variance equals true variance plus error variance.

q: What is the retention without conscious recollection of skills and dispositions called?
who: Daniel Schacter, implicit memory

concept.t: Implicit memory is retention shown in behaviour without conscious recollection, such as skills, habits and conditioned dispositions.
Riding a bicycle, typing, or feeling uneasy near dogs after a bite. Priming is also implicit: an earlier exposure speeds later recognition without awareness.
Amnesic patients such as H.M. (Henry Molaison) lose explicit memory but still learn new skills such as mirror drawing, showing the two systems are separate.

wrong.1: Iconic memory is the brief visual sensory store, lasting under a second, shown by George Sperling's partial report studies.
wrong.3: Explicit (declarative) memory is the opposite: facts and events that are consciously recalled.
wrong.4: Semantic memory, named by Endel Tulving, is consciously accessible general knowledge such as word meanings and facts, a part of explicit memory.

q: Arrange in sequence what Yerkes described commonly takes place in "insight learning". (A) Sharpening and frequent recurrent attention to the goal (B) Trial (C) Survey/Inspection (D) Attitude of concentrated attention (E) Critical point
who: Robert Yerkes, insight in great apes

concept.t: Robert Yerkes, watching apes solve problems, saw them first survey the situation, pause in concentrated attention, try a response, keep attending to the goal, and finally reach a critical point of sudden solution.
(C) Survey/inspection → (D) attitude of concentrated attention → (B) trial → (A) sharpening and recurrent attention to the goal → (E) critical point, after which the act is readily repeated.
Insight learning is linked with Wolfgang Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan, who joined sticks and stacked boxes to reach bananas. Insight is sudden, transfers well and is not blind trial and error.

wrong.1: Starts with trial, but in Yerkes' account the animal first surveys and inspects the problem; trial comes only after concentrated attention.
wrong.2: Starts with trial before survey; trial comes third, after inspection and a pause of concentrated attention.
wrong.4: Starts with trial and puts the critical point before concentrated attention; the critical point, the sudden solution, is the last step.

q: Who among the following is credited with proposing the investment theory of creativity?
who: Robert Sternberg and Todd Lubart, investment theory

concept.t: Robert Sternberg and Todd Lubart proposed the investment theory: creative people 'buy low and sell high', backing unpopular ideas and moving on once they become accepted.
Creativity needs six resources working together: intellectual abilities, knowledge, thinking styles, personality, motivation and environment.
Sternberg also gave the triarchic theory of intelligence and the triangular theory of love.

wrong.1: Jacob Getzels and Philip Jackson studied gifted school pupils and showed that high creativity and high IQ were only weakly related.
wrong.2: James Kaufman, with Ronald Beghetto, proposed the Four C model of creativity (mini-c, little-c, Pro-c, Big-C).
wrong.3: Michael Wallach and Nathan Kogan tested children's creativity in a relaxed, game-like, untimed setting and found it fairly separate from intelligence.

q: Which of the following principle is violated when a psychologist intentionally misrepresents his research results?
who: APA Ethics Code, Principle C: Integrity

concept.t: APA Principle C, Integrity, asks psychologists to promote accuracy, honesty and truthfulness. Knowingly misrepresenting results is dishonest, so it breaks integrity.
The APA Ethics Code has five general principles: (A) Beneficence and non-maleficence, (B) Fidelity and responsibility, (C) Integrity, (D) Justice, (E) Respect for people's rights and dignity.
Making up data is fabrication; presenting others' work as one's own is plagiarism; both are research misconduct.

wrong.1: Principle A, beneficence and non-maleficence, is about benefiting clients and avoiding harm, not about honesty in reporting.
wrong.2: Principle B, fidelity and responsibility, is about building trust and accepting professional responsibility towards clients and society.
wrong.4: Confidentiality is a specific standard about protecting client information, not one of the five general principles, and it is not about falsifying results.

q: In multiple approach-avoidance conflict, one has to choose between which of the following?
who: Kurt Lewin, types of motivational conflict

concept.t: In a multiple approach-avoidance conflict there are more than two options and each has both attractive and unattractive features, for example choosing between three job offers.
Approach-approach: two attractive goals; avoidance-avoidance: two unpleasant ones; approach-avoidance: one goal with good and bad sides; double approach-avoidance: two goals, each with both sides.
Kurt Lewin described the basic types. Approach-avoidance conflicts often cause vacillation, because avoidance rises faster than approach as the goal comes near.

wrong.1: This is a double approach-avoidance conflict: only two goals, each with good and bad sides.
wrong.3: Wrongly gives only one goal negative features; in the multiple form, every option has both positive and negative sides.
wrong.4: Allows some goals to be purely positive or purely negative; in multiple approach-avoidance every option has both sides.

q: Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Cancer that originates in the blood-forming cells such as stem cells (B) Cancer of the epithelial tissue, cells that line the outer and inner surface of the body such as skin, stomach etc. (C) Cancer that arises from the cells in connective tissue such as bone, muscles (D) Cancer of the sympathetic system which is one of the rare types of cancer. List II: (I) Carcinoma (II) Sarcoma (III) Leukaemia (IV) Lymphoma. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: As printed no option fits the true pairs A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV and D says 'sympathetic' for lymphatic; option 4 fits if the lists were reordered in copying, and option 1 (also only D right) is the runner-up.
who: Cancer types by tissue of origin

concept.t: As printed, no option is fully right; option (4) keeps D-IV (lymphoma) and shares pairs with every other option, so it is the most likely intended answer.

(A) Blood-forming cells = (III) Leukaemia; (B) Epithelial tissue = (I) Carcinoma; (C) Connective tissue such as bone and muscle = (II) Sarcoma; (D) Lymphatic system ('sympathetic' is a copying slip) = (IV) Lymphoma.
Carcinomas are by far the most common type. Hooks: sarc = flesh (Greek sarx), leuk = white (white blood cells), lymph = the lymphatic system.

wrong.1: Matches D correctly but gives blood-forming cells to sarcoma and epithelium to leukaemia; sarcoma arises in connective tissue such as bone and muscle.
wrong.2: Gets every pair wrong as printed: it calls the connective tissue cancer lymphoma and the lymphatic cancer leukaemia.
wrong.3: Gets every pair wrong as printed: it calls the blood-forming cancer lymphoma and the lymphatic cancer carcinoma, which is a cancer of epithelial tissue.

q: Which of the following characterise the hardy person? (A) He is high on sense of commitment (B) He is more likely to act to 'cover-up' (C) He doesn't avoid problems, yet he is often angry (D) He is always under the control of his life and events
who: Suzanne Kobasa, hardiness (commitment, control, challenge)

concept.t: Suzanne Kobasa found that hardy people combine commitment, a sense of control over life events, and seeing change as a challenge. A is commitment; D, read as being in control of one's life, is control.
Hardiness buffers stress: highly stressed executives high in hardiness fell ill less often. Hardy people use active, transformational coping instead of avoiding or denying problems.
Remember the three Cs: commitment, control, challenge. Hostility and anger belong to the toxic core of the Type A pattern, not to hardiness.

wrong.1: Statement C is false: hardy people face problems, but frequent anger and hostility mark the Type A pattern, which raises heart disease risk.
wrong.3: Statement B is false: covering up or denying problems is avoidant coping, the opposite of the active coping hardy people use.
wrong.4: Commitment and control fit, but statement B does not: hardy people face and transform problems rather than covering them up.

q: A researcher is studying the group process of software startup developers by staying with them for six months. Which of the following is used by her?
who: Ethnography, John Creswell's five qualitative approaches

concept.t: Ethnography studies the shared patterns of a culture-sharing group through long fieldwork, living with and observing the group. Staying six months with a startup team to study its group process fits exactly.
The main method is participant observation, backed by interviews and field notes. It grew out of anthropological fieldwork.

John Creswell's five approaches: narrative (one person's story), phenomenology (lived experience), grounded theory (build a theory), ethnography (a culture-sharing group), case study (a bounded case).

wrong.1: Grounded theory (Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss) aims to build a new theory from data through coding and constant comparison, not to describe a group's culture.
wrong.3: Narrative analysis studies the life stories of one or a few individuals and retells them in time order.
wrong.4: Phenomenological research describes the shared lived experience of a phenomenon, such as grief, across several people, mainly through in-depth interviews.

q: What do you call the neurological procedure involving the implantation of a medical device under the skin in the chest that sends electrical impulses to electrodes surgically placed in a specific location in the brain?
who: Deep brain stimulation (DBS)

concept.t: In deep brain stimulation a pulse generator, like a pacemaker, is placed under the skin of the chest and wired to electrodes implanted deep in the brain.
It is used for Parkinson's disease, essential tremor and dystonia, and is being studied for severe, treatment-resistant OCD and depression. A common target is the subthalamic nucleus.
Chest device + electrodes in the brain = DBS; chest device + wire to a neck nerve = VNS; magnetic coil on the scalp = rTMS.

wrong.2: rTMS is non-invasive: a magnetic coil held against the scalp induces currents in the cortex, and nothing is implanted.
wrong.3: ECT passes a brief current through scalp electrodes under anaesthesia to cause a controlled seizure; nothing is implanted.
wrong.4: VNS also uses a chest pulse generator, but its wire goes to the vagus nerve in the neck, not to electrodes inside the brain.

q: According to Lazarus, what comes between the stimulus and the emotional response to that stimulus to mediate?
who: Richard Lazarus, cognitive appraisal theory

concept.t: Richard Lazarus held that emotion depends on how we judge an event. This cognitive appraisal sits between the stimulus and the emotional response.
Primary appraisal asks whether the event is relevant, harmful or threatening; secondary appraisal asks whether I can cope. Reappraisal updates the judgement.
Lazarus debated Robert Zajonc, who claimed that feeling can come before thinking (affective primacy).

wrong.1: Physiological reactions come first in the James-Lange theory, where emotion is the perception of bodily changes.
wrong.2: Labelling of arousal is the central step in Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory.
wrong.3: In the two-factor theory, Schachter and Singer said people use social and situational cues to label unexplained arousal; Lazarus stressed appraisal of the event's meaning instead.

q: Several types of heuristics have been identified by researchers. Which of these are included in it? (A) Lexicographic strategy (B) Satisficing strategy (C) Mental set (D) Elimination by aspects
who: Decision heuristics: Herbert Simon, Amos Tversky

concept.t: The lexicographic strategy, satisficing and elimination by aspects are short-cut decision rules, that is, heuristics. Mental set is a problem-solving block, not a decision heuristic.

Lexicographic: choose the option that is best on the single most important attribute; satisficing (Herbert Simon): take the first option that is good enough; elimination by aspects (Amos Tversky): drop options that fail on one attribute at a time.
Mental set is shown in Abraham Luchins' water jar problems: people keep using a method that worked before even when a simpler one exists.

wrong.1: Includes mental set, a fixed way of approaching problems that blocks new solutions, and leaves out elimination by aspects.
wrong.3: Leaves out satisficing, Herbert Simon's rule of taking the first good-enough option, and wrongly includes mental set.
wrong.4: Leaves out the lexicographic strategy and wrongly includes mental set, which is a barrier to problem solving.

q: Which one of the following is the correct description of Old Fashioned Racism?
who: John McConahay, old-fashioned versus modern racism

concept.t: Old-fashioned racism is open, blatant prejudice: beliefs in racial superiority, support for segregation and formal, legal discrimination.
After the civil rights era open racism became socially unacceptable and gave way to subtler forms such as modern racism, measured by John McConahay's Modern Racism Scale.
Blatant = old-fashioned; values not self-interest = symbolic; egalitarian values plus avoidance = aversive; automatic associations = implicit.

wrong.1: This describes symbolic racism (David Sears), a modern form rooted in values such as individualism rather than personal self-interest.
wrong.3: This describes aversive racism (Samuel Gaertner and John Dovidio): egalitarian beliefs plus hidden negative feelings that lead to avoidance.
wrong.4: This describes implicit prejudice or stereotypes: automatic associations, measured with tools like the Implicit Association Test.

q: Match List I with List II. List I (Description): (A) A laboratory device for testing depth in infants and young animals (B) Refers to the differences in two eyes' location of corner angles (C) Refers to two points which fall on non-corresponding retinal positions one nearer and the other farther (D) Perceptional adaptability to adjust to an artificially displaced visual field. List II (Concept): (I) Perceptual adaptation (II) Horizontal disparity (III) Vertical disparity (IV) Visual cliff. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk, visual cliff; binocular disparity

concept.t: The visual cliff tests depth perception in infants and perceptual adaptation is adjusting to a displaced visual field; only option (4) has both. B and C are the two kinds of binocular disparity.

(A) Depth test for infants = (IV) Visual cliff; (B) Different positions of corners and angles in the two eyes = (III) Vertical disparity; (C) Points on non-corresponding retinal positions, nearer or farther = (II) Horizontal disparity; (D) Adjusting to a displaced field = (I) Perceptual adaptation.

Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk found most crawling infants would not cross the 'deep' side of the cliff. Horizontal disparity is the main cue for stereopsis, and people wearing prism goggles that shift the visual field soon adapt their reaching.

wrong.1: Puts perceptual adaptation on the infant depth test and the visual cliff on the displaced field; the visual cliff is Gibson and Walk's infant depth test.
wrong.2: Gets D right but gives the infant depth device to horizontal disparity and the retinal-position description to the visual cliff.
wrong.3: Gives the infant depth test to vertical disparity and the displaced field to horizontal disparity; these are the visual cliff and perceptual adaptation.

q: Which one of the following branches of philosophy of science deals with the question of existence?
who: Ontology, the study of being

concept.t: Ontology is the branch of philosophy that asks what exists and what kinds of things are real. In science it asks which entities (atoms, minds, traits) truly exist.
Ontology asks "what is there?"; epistemology asks "how do we know it?"; methodology asks "how do we study it?".
Research paradigms are compared on these three. Positivism assumes one real world (realist ontology); constructivism assumes reality is socially built (relativist ontology).

wrong.1: A research paradigm holding that reality exists but can only be known imperfectly, so claims are probabilistic and open to falsification; it is a position, not the branch about existence.
wrong.2: A school of thought that breaks things into basic elements or underlying structures (Edward Titchener in psychology), not the philosophical study of existence.
wrong.4: A specific position within the debate, not a branch: it holds that the unobservable entities of successful theories, such as electrons or genes, really exist.

q: Which of the following is the correct response pattern for the semantic differential test to measure a trait 'active'?
who: Charles Osgood, semantic differential (1957)

concept.t: Charles Osgood's semantic differential rates a concept on a line between two bipolar adjectives, such as active and passive, usually with seven steps and a neutral middle.
Ratings group into three factors: evaluation (good to bad), potency (strong to weak) and activity (active to passive). "Active versus passive" is an activity scale.
Opposite adjectives with steps between = Osgood; strongly agree to strongly disagree = Likert; true or false = inventory format such as the MMPI.

wrong.1: This is the Likert (summated ratings) format: agreement with a statement on five steps from strongly agree to strongly disagree.
wrong.2: A dichotomous true/false item format, as used in inventories such as the MMPI, not a scale between two opposite adjectives.
wrong.3: Active and trusting are not opposites, so this is a forced choice between two unrelated traits, not a bipolar semantic scale.

q: Which approach focussed on the nature of a task and its influence on a person's ability in solving problems?
doubt: Gestalt psychologists also stressed how the structure of a problem shapes its solution (restructuring, functional fixedness), so (3) is the runner-up.
who: Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, information processing approach

concept.t: Allen Newell and Herbert Simon analysed the task environment: the structure of the task sets what the solver must represent and which moves are possible.
The solver builds a problem space (start state, goal state, operators) and searches it with heuristics such as means-end analysis, limited by working memory capacity.
Associationist = trial and error, habit strength; Gestalt = restructuring and insight; information processing = task analysis, problem space and computer simulation (General Problem Solver).

wrong.1: Explains problem solving as trial and error that strengthens stimulus-response bonds (Edward Thorndike), so it focuses on learned habits rather than the structure of the task.
wrong.3: Wolfgang Köhler, Max Wertheimer and Karl Duncker stressed perceptual restructuring, sudden insight and blocks such as functional fixedness, not a formal analysis of the task.
wrong.4: Treats problem solving as responses shaped by reinforcement history and ignores how the solver mentally represents the task.

q: Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Pratibha (B) Prajna (C) Vak (D) Bhavas. List II: (I) Samkhya philosophy (II) Nyaya Vaisesika (III) Tantrik tradition (IV) Patanjali Yoga system. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Classical Indian philosophical systems (darshanas) and Tantra

concept.t: (A) Pratibha = (II) Nyaya Vaisesika; (B) Prajna = (IV) Patanjali Yoga system; (C) Vak = (III) Tantrik tradition; (D) Bhavas = (I) Samkhya philosophy.
Pratibha is a flash of intuitive knowledge that arises without the senses, discussed in Nyaya Vaisesika as the knowledge of seers. Prajna in the Yoga Sutras is insight wisdom reached in samadhi.
In Tantra, vak (speech) unfolds in levels from para to vaikhari (spoken word). In Samkhya, the eight bhavas are dispositions of buddhi: virtue, knowledge, detachment, power and their opposites.

wrong.1: Every pair is wrong: pratibha belongs to Nyaya Vaisesika, prajna to Yoga, vak to the Tantrik tradition and the bhavas to Samkhya.
wrong.2: Gets pratibha and prajna right but swaps the last two: vak belongs to the Tantrik tradition and the bhavas to Samkhya.
wrong.4: Only prajna (Yoga) is right; pratibha is Nyaya Vaisesika, vak is Tantrik and the bhavas are Samkhya.

q: In the famous experiment by Schachter and Singer involving epinephrine, what was found to govern the emotions?
who: Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer, two-factor theory (1962)

concept.t: In Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer's two-factor theory, emotion needs both physiological arousal and a cognitive label (appraisal) explaining why one is aroused.

Participants got epinephrine. Those not told about its side effects took on the mood of a euphoric or angry stooge, labelling their arousal from the situation; informed participants blamed the drug and copied less.
James-Lange = bodily change first, then emotion; Cannon-Bard = both at once via the thalamus; Schachter-Singer = arousal plus label.

wrong.1: Cues from the situation guided the labelling, but on their own they did not produce emotion; arousal from the drug was also needed.
wrong.2: The stooge's behaviour supplied the cue for labelling, but the theory also requires physiological arousal, so social appraisal alone is not enough.
wrong.4: Leaves out the bodily factor; the core claim is that arousal must be present and then explained cognitively.

q: Who among the following has laid emphasis on examining the relationship of culturally specific practices with development?
who: Lev Vygotsky, sociocultural theory

concept.t: Lev Vygotsky argued that development cannot be separated from its cultural and social context: the tools, language and practices of a culture shape how children think.

Children learn through interaction with more skilled people within the zone of proximal development, supported by scaffolding. Higher mental functions appear first between people, then within the child.
Piaget = child as lone scientist passing universal stages; Vygotsky = child as apprentice whose path depends on culture.

wrong.1: Jean Piaget proposed universal stages driven by the child's own exploration and gave culture only a minor role.
wrong.2: Jerry Fodor is a philosopher of mind known for the modularity of mind and the language of thought, not cultural development.
wrong.4: Lawrence Kohlberg proposed universal stages of moral reasoning and has been criticised for underplaying cultural variation.

q: Mr A is very good at discriminating between progressive and regressive ways of behaviour. His choices are clearly perceived by him and adequately symbolised. According to Rogers, these are the characteristics of which of the following? (A) Individual tendency towards 'growth' (B) Tendency to 'self actualise' (C) His constructive creativity (D) His self-affirmation
who: Carl Rogers, actualising tendency

concept.t: Carl Rogers held that the forward-moving growth tendency, the drive to self-actualise, works only when choices are clearly perceived and adequately symbolised. A person must tell progressive from regressive behaviour to actualise.
The actualising tendency is the one master motive to maintain and enhance the organism, moving it towards greater differentiation, autonomy and maturity.
Denied or distorted experience (incongruence) blurs this choice; congruence lets the person see and take the growth path.

wrong.1: Includes (C) and drops (B); Rogers ties clear symbolisation of choices to the tendency to self-actualise, not to creativity as such.
wrong.2: Adds (C) and (D) and drops (B); creativity and self-affirmation are not what Rogers links to telling progressive from regressive behaviour.
wrong.4: Self-actualising is right, but Rogers describes it as the forward-moving growth tendency, so (A) belongs with it.

q: For an intelligence test in an educational setting, which of the following difficulty value shows maximum discrimination?
who: Item difficulty index and discrimination

concept.t: An item passed by 50% (p = 0.5) splits the group into two equal halves, giving the largest number of pass-fail contrasts between people, so it discriminates most.
Item difficulty p is the proportion who answer correctly. At p = 1.0 or 0 everyone gets the same result, so the item tells you nothing about differences.
Anne Anastasi: for maximum differentiation choose items near p = 0.5. With guessing on multiple choice the optimum rises to about (1 + chance)/2, for example 0.625 for four options.

wrong.1: An easy item: 80% pass, so it only separates the weakest fifth from the rest and makes fewer distinctions between people.
wrong.2: Close to the optimum and near the value adjusted for guessing on four-option items, but without that adjustment 0.5 discriminates more.
wrong.4: A hard item: only 30% pass, so most people fail it and it separates fewer pairs of test takers.

q: Making decisions by the use of mental short cuts that focus on one aspect of a problem, while ignoring others refers to which one of the following?
who: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, heuristics

concept.t: Heuristics are mental shortcuts or rules of thumb that give fast answers by using only part of the information, so they can bias decisions.
Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described availability (judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind), representativeness (judging by resemblance to a prototype) and anchoring.
Heuristic = quick but error-prone; algorithm = step-by-step method that guarantees a solution but is slow.

wrong.1: The effect of how options are worded (as gains or as losses) on the choice people make, shown by Tversky and Kahneman.
wrong.2: Clinging to a belief even after the evidence for it has been discredited.
wrong.4: A tendency to keep using a strategy that worked before even when a better one exists, as in Abraham Luchins' water jar problems.

q: Which of the following are the parts of mental logic theories of reasoning? (A) A set of inference schemas (B) Accumulation of concepts (C) A reasoning program (D) A set of pragmatic principles
who: Martin Braine and David O'Brien, mental logic theory

concept.t: Mental logic theories, such as that of Martin Braine and David O'Brien, have three parts: a set of inference schemas, a reasoning program that applies them, and pragmatic principles that shape how premises are understood.
People are assumed to carry abstract rules such as modus ponens in the head; the program chains them to reach conclusions, while pragmatic principles handle context and wording.
Mental logic (Braine; Lance Rips' PSYCOP) = rules of inference; mental models (Philip Johnson-Laird) = imagined scenarios of the premises.

wrong.1: Includes (B) and drops (D); accumulation of concepts is not a component, while pragmatic principles are.
wrong.2: Includes (B) and drops (C); the reasoning program that applies the schemas is a core part of the theory.
wrong.4: Drops (A), the inference schemas that are the heart of any mental logic theory, and adds (B), which is not a part.

q: In which sequence, according to Piaget, are the following cognitive milestones achieved? (A) Object permanence (B) Reversibility (C) Abstraction (D) Centration
who: Jean Piaget, stages of cognitive development

concept.t: (A) Object permanence, sensorimotor (0 to 2 years) → (D) Centration, preoperational (2 to 7) → (B) Reversibility, concrete operational (7 to 11) → (C) Abstraction, formal operational (11 onwards).

Object permanence: knowing objects exist when unseen. Centration: attending to one feature only, such as water height. Reversibility: mentally undoing an action, which allows conservation. Abstraction: reasoning about hypothetical ideas.
Jean Piaget saw centration as a limit of preoperational thought, overcome by decentration and reversibility in the concrete stage.

wrong.1: Puts reversibility before centration; centration is a preoperational limit that reversibility later overcomes.
wrong.2: Starts with abstraction, the last formal operational achievement, and ends with centration, a preoperational feature.
wrong.3: Puts centration before object permanence, but object permanence develops in infancy, before preoperational thought.

q: Arrange the following in sequence as per the Excitation Transfer Theory of Aggression. (A) Frustration (B) Residual Arousal (C) Arousing Events (D) Increased Arousal (E) Arousal attributed to Frustration
who: Dolf Zillmann, excitation transfer theory

concept.t: (C) Arousing event, such as exercise → (D) Increased arousal → (B) Residual arousal that lingers → (A) A new frustration → (E) Leftover arousal attributed to the frustration, which intensifies aggression.
Dolf Zillmann argued that physiological arousal fades slowly, so arousal from one source can transfer to a later situation. If the person does not notice it, they misattribute it to the provocation.
The effect is strongest when the person is unaware of the leftover arousal; it builds on Schachter's two-factor idea of labelling arousal.

wrong.1: Starts with frustration, but the unrelated arousing event comes first; frustration is the later trigger onto which residual arousal is transferred.
wrong.2: Begins with increased arousal before the event that caused it and puts residual arousal before the arousing event.
wrong.4: Starts with frustration; in the theory the earlier arousing event comes first, and frustration arrives only after arousal has become residual.

q: Arrange the stages of personality development in the theory given by Rollo May. (A) Innocence (B) Rebellion (C) Ordinary consciousness of self (D) Creative consciousness of self
who: Rollo May, existential stages of development

concept.t: (A) Innocence (infancy) → (B) Rebellion (childhood and adolescence) → (C) Ordinary consciousness of self → (D) Creative consciousness of self.

Innocence: acting on instinct without self-awareness. Rebellion: wanting freedom without accepting its responsibility. Ordinary consciousness: learning from mistakes and living responsibly. Creative consciousness: rare moments of seeing beyond everyday limits.
Rollo May, an American existential psychologist, treated these as forms of consciousness rather than strict age stages; few adults reach the creative level.

wrong.1: Puts ordinary consciousness of self before rebellion, but rebellion against parents and authority comes first, in childhood and adolescence.
wrong.3: Starts with rebellion, but the innocence of infancy comes before any wish for independence.
wrong.4: Puts innocence last, but innocence is the first, infant stage.

q: Which of the following internal roadblocks to effective listening is exemplified by the statement "We have never done it that way before"? (A) Resistance to change (B) Halo Effect (C) Stereotyping (D) Hearing only, not feeling
who: Internal roadblocks to effective listening

concept.t: "We have never done it that way before" shows resistance to change: the listener rejects a new idea because it differs from habit, without really hearing it.
Internal roadblocks are barriers inside the listener, such as fixed attitudes, bias and emotional reactions, that stop the message being understood.
Halo effect = judging the message by one liked or disliked trait of the speaker; stereotyping = judging it by the speaker's group.

wrong.2: Adds the halo effect, letting one overall impression of the speaker colour the whole message; the statement is about an unfamiliar idea, not the speaker.
wrong.3: Adds the halo effect and stereotyping, which both judge the speaker; the statement rejects an idea only because it is new.
wrong.4: Also adds hearing only, not feeling (taking in words but missing the speaker's emotions), which the statement does not show.

q: Which of the following are associated with the Path in Sufism? (A) Establishing self and assertion (B) Repentance (C) Renunciation (D) Poverty (E) Annihilation
who: Sufi tariqa: stations (maqamat) of the Path

concept.t: The Sufi Path (tariqa) passes through stations (maqamat) such as repentance (tawba), renunciation (zuhd), poverty (faqr), patience and trust in God, and ends in annihilation (fana) of the ego in God.
The Path aims to dissolve the lower self (nafs), so establishing and asserting the self is the opposite of the Sufi goal.
Fana (passing away of self) is followed by baqa (abiding in God). Maqamat are stations earned by effort; ahwal are states given by God.

wrong.1: Repentance, renunciation and annihilation fit, but it leaves out poverty (faqr), a classic station of the Path.
wrong.2: Includes self-assertion, the opposite of the Path's aim of effacing the ego, and leaves out renunciation and annihilation.
wrong.3: Includes self-assertion and leaves out annihilation (fana), the final goal of the Path.

q: A group of sixty newly diagnosed diabetic patients were tested for anxiety using a standardized inventory. They were retested for anxiety again after some months using the same inventory. The mean difference in anxiety was evaluated by a suitable t-test. The degrees of freedom associated with the t-test would be
who: Paired samples t-test, df = n - 1

concept.t: The same 60 patients are measured twice, so this is a paired (dependent) t-test. It works on 60 difference scores, giving df = n - 1 = 60 - 1 = 59.
Each patient's retest score is subtracted from the first score; t = mean difference ÷ (SD of differences ÷ √n), read with n - 1 degrees of freedom.
Two independent groups: df = n1 + n2 - 2. Paired or one-sample t: df = n - 1. Testing a correlation: df = n - 2.

wrong.1: The total number of scores (60 × 2), not degrees of freedom; it wrongly treats the retest as 60 new people.
wrong.2: This is n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> - 2 for two independent groups of 60, but here one group is retested.
wrong.4: Subtracts 2 from a single group; df = n - 2 applies when testing a correlation, not a paired t-test.

q: Which of the following is true about Hypovolemia? (A) It causes thirst (B) It increases the blood pressure (C) Angiotensin is released during this condition (D) The volume of blood increases (E) Blood pressure reduces
who: Volumetric thirst and the renin-angiotensin system

concept.t: Hypovolemia is low blood volume, as after bleeding or diarrhoea. Blood pressure falls, the kidneys release renin, which forms angiotensin II, and this triggers volumetric thirst. So (A), (C) and (E) are true.
Both are reversed: in hypovolemia blood volume has dropped, so blood pressure falls rather than rises.
Angiotensin II constricts blood vessels, releases aldosterone to retain sodium and acts on the subfornical organ to cause thirst. Baroreceptors in the heart and vessels also detect the drop.
Osmotic thirst = cells lose water to salty extracellular fluid; volumetric thirst = loss of blood volume.

wrong.1: Includes (B), but low blood volume lowers blood pressure; it does not raise it.
wrong.3: Includes (D), but hypovolemia means blood volume has fallen, not increased.
wrong.4: Includes (B) and (D), both reversed: blood pressure and blood volume drop in hypovolemia.

q: Testing the scientific hypothesis is impossible due to the need of auxiliary assumptions. What is this associated with?
who: Pierre Duhem and Willard Van Orman Quine, confirmation holism

concept.t: The Duhem-Quine thesis (Pierre Duhem, Willard Van Orman Quine) says a hypothesis is never tested alone but together with auxiliary assumptions about instruments, conditions and background theory.
When a prediction fails, logic cannot tell which part is wrong, so no single experiment decisively refutes a hypothesis. This is a problem for Karl Popper's falsificationism.
Also called confirmation holism: theories face evidence as a whole network, not one statement at a time.

wrong.1: The principle of parsimony, linked to William of Ockham: prefer the simplest explanation that fits the facts.
wrong.2: The Vienna Circle view that meaningful statements must be verifiable by observation, which assumed hypotheses could be checked fairly directly.
wrong.4: Thomas Kuhn and Paul Feyerabend's idea that rival paradigms lack a common measure, so they cannot be compared point by point.

q: Which one of the following attitude scaling methods is especially unsuitable for scaling a large number of attitude statements?
who: Louis Thurstone, method of paired comparisons

concept.t: In paired comparison, every statement is compared with every other, so n statements need n(n - 1)/2 judgements: 20 statements need 190 pairs and 50 need 1,225, which is unmanageable.
Judges pick the more favourable statement in each pair; the proportions are turned into scale values using Louis Thurstone's law of comparative judgement.
Sorting methods (equal appearing and successive intervals) cope with large item pools; Rensis Likert's summated ratings are the quickest to build.

wrong.2: Thurstone's sorting method: judges place each statement once into one of 11 ordered piles, so it handles many statements easily.
wrong.3: Rensis Likert's method: each statement is rated once on agree to disagree steps, so large item pools are no problem.
wrong.4: Also sorts each statement once into ordered categories without pairing, so it suits large sets of statements.

q: Which one of the following personality test/s employ/s a 'Lie' scale? (A) Rotter's Locus of control scale (B) Eysenck Personality Profiler (C) Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory-2 (D) Edwards Personal Preference Schedule
who: Lie scales as validity checks in inventories

concept.t: The MMPI-2 has the L (Lie) scale among its validity scales. Hans Eysenck's Eysenck Personality Profiler, like the EPQ, includes a lie scale to catch people presenting themselves too favourably.
Lie items describe small faults almost everyone has ("I sometimes get angry"); denying many of them suggests the person is faking good.
Julian Rotter's I-E scale uses filler items to hide its purpose. Allen Edwards' EPPS controls social desirability with matched forced-choice pairs and a consistency score, not a lie scale.

wrong.1: The MMPI-2 does have the L scale, but the Eysenck Personality Profiler also has a lie scale, so (C) alone is incomplete.
wrong.3: Includes Rotter's I-E scale and the EPPS, neither of which has a lie scale, and leaves out the MMPI-2.
wrong.4: Includes the EPPS, which handles faking with matched forced-choice pairs and a consistency score rather than a lie scale.

q: Which of the following statements are true about Unity Thema? (A) It is a compound of interrelated needs linked to press (B) It is a compound of conflicting needs linked to press (C) It operates largely as an unconscious force (D) It operates largely as a conscious force
who: Henry Murray, unity thema

concept.t: Henry Murray defined the unity thema as a compound of interrelated, collaborating or conflicting dominant needs linked to press met in early childhood, so (A) and (B) are both true.
The thema forms from a gratifying or traumatic childhood experience and then shapes much of later behaviour. It operates largely as an unconscious force, so (C) is true and (D) false.
Need plus press = thema; the unity thema is the single underlying pattern that gives a life its coherence.

wrong.2: Leaves out (B); Murray's definition covers collaborating or conflicting needs, so conflict among needs is part of the unity thema.
wrong.3: Includes (D), but Murray said the unity thema works largely outside awareness, not as a conscious force.
wrong.4: Includes (D) and drops (A) and (C); the thema is largely unconscious and its needs are interrelated.

q: Match List I with List II. List I (Description): (A) A reinforcement that reinforces a response at unpredictable time intervals (B) A reinforcement that reinforces a response only after a specified time has lapsed (C) A reinforcement that reinforces a response after an unpredictable number of responses (D) A reinforcement that reinforces a response only after a specified number of responses. List II (Type of Reinforcement): (I) Fixed-ratio schedule (II) Variable-ratio schedule (III) Fixed-interval schedule (IV) Variable-interval schedule. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: B. F. Skinner, schedules of reinforcement

concept.t: (A) Unpredictable time = (IV) variable-interval; (B) set time lapse = (III) fixed-interval; (C) unpredictable number of responses = (II) variable-ratio; (D) set number of responses = (I) fixed-ratio.
In B. F. Skinner's partial schedules, ratio depends on the number of responses and interval on time since the last reinforcer. Fixed = same each time; variable = changes around an average.
Variable-ratio (slot machines) gives the highest, steadiest rate and most resistance to extinction; fixed-interval gives a scallop, with responding speeding up as reward time nears.

wrong.1: Every pair is wrong: it gives the time-based descriptions to ratio schedules and the response-count descriptions to interval schedules.
wrong.2: Gets (B) and (D) right but swaps (A) and (C): unpredictable time is variable-interval and an unpredictable number of responses is variable-ratio.
wrong.3: Every pair is wrong; for example, a set number of responses is fixed-ratio, not variable-ratio, and a set time lapse is fixed-interval.

q: Which of the following is the correct explanation of "An intolerance for weakness, a punitive attitude and submissive respect for their in-group authorities as reflected in their agreement"?
doubt: The traits described are those of the authoritarian personality, which is not offered; social dominance orientation (1) is the nearest rival construct, but textbooks attach these traits to ethnocentric people.
who: Theodor Adorno et al., The Authoritarian Personality (1950)

concept.t: Theodor Adorno and colleagues found that people prejudiced against one minority were prejudiced against most outgroups (ethnocentrism). These ethnocentric people shared authoritarian tendencies: intolerance for weakness, a punitive attitude and submissive respect for in-group authorities.

Ethnocentrism is belief in the superiority of one's own group with contempt for outgroups. The F scale measured the authoritarian traits behind it, with items like "Obedience and respect for authority are the most important virtues children should learn".
Authoritarianism = submission to in-group authority plus hostility to outgroups; social dominance orientation = wanting one's group to dominate others.

wrong.1: Jim Sidanius and Felicia Pratto's preference for group hierarchy, with one's own group on top; it is about dominance, not submission to in-group authority.
wrong.3: Changing behaviour or belief to match a group, as in Solomon Asch's line studies; a general social influence process, not a prejudiced personality pattern.
wrong.4: The unequal spread of status and resources in a society; it describes social structure, not a set of personal attitudes.

q: Vaibhasika and Sautrantika are associated with which of the following?
who: Sarvastivada schools of Buddhist Abhidharma

concept.t: Vaibhasika and Sautrantika are the two schools of the Sarvastivada (Hinayana) tradition. Vaibhasika follows the Mahavibhasa commentary; Sautrantika relies on the sutras rather than the Abhidharma.
Both are realist. Vaibhasikas hold that external objects are perceived directly (direct realism); Sautrantikas hold that they are only inferred from mental images (representationalism).
Four classic Buddhist schools: Vaibhasika and Sautrantika (Hinayana, realist); Yogacara (Mahayana, mind-only) and Madhyamika (Mahayana, emptiness).

wrong.1: The surviving Pali school of Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, a Hinayana lineage separate from the Sarvastivada.
wrong.2: The mental factors (such as attention, feeling, greed) listed in Theravada Abhidhamma psychology; a category of mind, not a school.
wrong.3: Nagarjuna's Mahayana school of emptiness (shunyata), which criticised the realism of the Sarvastivadins.

q: Adult neurons rely heavily on which of the following? (A) Glucose (B) Protein (C) Potassium (D) Sodium
doubt: Neurons also depend on sodium and potassium gradients for signalling, so (4) is defensible if the stem means more than fuel.
who: Neuronal energy metabolism: glucose dependence

concept.t: Adult neurons use glucose almost exclusively as fuel and store very little of it, so they need a steady supply from the blood. The brain uses about a fifth of the body's energy.
Glucose is carried across the blood-brain barrier by transporter proteins; using it needs oxygen and thiamine (vitamin B1). Low blood sugar quickly impairs brain function.
In starvation the brain can partly switch to ketone bodies, but in normal adult life glucose is its main fuel. Sodium and potassium are signalling ions, not fuel.

wrong.2: Neurons use protein to build structures, enzymes and neurotransmitters, but not as their main energy source.
wrong.3: These ions create the resting potential and action potentials, but they are pumped, not used as fuel; the sodium-potassium pump itself runs on ATP made from glucose.
wrong.4: Glucose is right, but sodium and potassium are needed for signalling rather than relied on for energy.

q: Johnson-Laird (1995) has some contingencies in the scientific study of logic, which comprise: (A) Relational inferences (B) Propositional inferences (C) Focus gambling (D) Syllogisms
who: Philip Johnson-Laird, mental models theory of deduction

concept.t: Philip Johnson-Laird reviewed the study of deduction under three kinds of inference: relational inferences, propositional inferences and syllogisms. Focus gambling is not a form of logic at all.
Relational: 'A is taller than B, B is taller than C, so A is taller than C'. Propositional: built on if, or, and, not; syllogisms: two quantified premises ('All A are B') and a conclusion.
In his mental models theory, people build a mental picture of what the premises describe and read the conclusion off it. Problems that need more models are harder and cause more errors.
Focus gambling is a concept-attainment strategy from Jerome Bruner, Jacqueline Goodnow and George Austin (1956), alongside conservative focusing and scanning.

wrong.1: Includes focus gambling, a concept-attainment strategy from Jerome Bruner's work, and leaves out syllogisms, a core domain of deduction.
wrong.3: Drops propositional inferences (reasoning with if, or, not), one of the three domains, and adds focus gambling, which is not a type of logical inference.
wrong.4: Drops relational inferences such as transitive reasoning (A taller than B, B taller than C), and adds focus gambling, a concept-learning strategy.

q: Which is true about coefficient alpha? (A) It is a lower bound of a test of parallel items (B) It is an upper bound of a test of parallel items (C) It is an average of all combinations of split-half reliabilities (D) It is independent of inter-item correlations
who: Lee Cronbach, coefficient alpha (1951)

concept.t: Coefficient alpha is a lower bound to a test's true reliability (A), and Lee Cronbach showed it equals the mean of all possible split-half coefficients (C).
Alpha estimates internal consistency, how far the items measure the same thing. It rises with the number of items and with the average inter-item correlation.
Alpha equals true reliability only when items are parallel or essentially tau-equivalent. When items differ, it tends to underestimate reliability, so it is treated as a floor.
KR-20 is the special case of alpha for items scored right or wrong (0 or 1).

wrong.1: C is true, but A is true as well: alpha is the standard lower-bound estimate of reliability, so C alone is incomplete.
wrong.2: B is false: alpha is a lower bound of reliability, not an upper bound, so A and B cannot both hold.
wrong.4: D is false: alpha is computed from inter-item covariances, so it rises as the items correlate more highly with one another.

q: Which of the following are considered in favour of scientific realism? (A) Corroboration (B) Empiricism (C) Miracle argument (D) Selective optimism
who: Hilary Putnam's no-miracles argument; selective realism

concept.t: Corroboration, the no-miracles argument and selective optimism are all moves realists make. Empiricism is the main anti-realist rival, so every option containing B fails.
Scientific realism holds that mature, successful theories are approximately true and that unobservable entities, such as electrons, really exist.

Hilary Putnam: the success of science would be a miracle if its theories were not roughly true. Corroboration: independent methods agreeing on the same entity is unlikely by chance; selective optimism: trust the parts of past theories that did the predictive work.
Bas van Fraassen's constructive empiricism says science aims only at empirical adequacy (truth about observables), so it argues against realism.

wrong.1: Includes empiricism, the anti-realist view (for example Bas van Fraassen's constructive empiricism) that science need only be true to observables, and omits the no-miracles argument.
wrong.2: Includes empiricism, which argues against realism, and omits corroboration and the no-miracles argument, the best-known case for realism.
wrong.3: The no-miracles argument fits, but empiricism is the leading anti-realist position, not a defence of realism.

q: In depth perception, what kind of images are used?
who: Depth perception from two-dimensional retinal images

concept.t: The image on each retina is flat, two-dimensional. Depth perception is the brain's ability to build a three-dimensional world from these 2D images.

The brain compares the two eyes' slightly different images through binocular cues (retinal disparity, convergence). It also uses monocular cues such as linear perspective, interposition, texture gradient and relative size.
The third dimension is the output of perception, not the input: the input is two flat images, one per eye.

wrong.1: A line has only one dimension; the retina receives a full flat image with height and width, not a line.
wrong.3: This is what we perceive, not what the eye receives; the brain infers the third dimension from cues in flat retinal images.
wrong.4: Vision has no such image type; time is sometimes called the fourth dimension, while depth is the third spatial dimension, built from flat images.

q: In the independent groups' design, selective subject loss occurs because of which of the following? (A) Subjects are lost differently across conditions (B) Subject characteristics are responsible for subject loss (C) Subjects are lost uniformly across conditions (D) Subject characteristics are independent of subject loss
who: John Shaughnessy and Eugene Zechmeister, Research Methods in Psychology

concept.t: Selective subject loss happens when participants drop out differently across conditions (A) and a subject characteristic linked to the outcome causes the dropout (B).

Random assignment made the groups equivalent, but losing, say, the least able people from a hard condition leaves groups that differ before the treatment acts. The independent variable is then confounded.
Mechanical subject loss (equipment failure, experimenter error) has nothing to do with the person, so it does not bias the groups.

wrong.2: C contradicts A: loss spread evenly across conditions leaves the groups comparable, so it is not selective loss.
wrong.3: D is the opposite of B: if subject characteristics were unrelated to dropping out, the loss would not bias the groups.
wrong.4: Both C and D describe loss that leaves the groups equivalent, which is harmless, unbiased loss, the opposite of selective loss.

q: Immediately after an action potential, the cell does not produce another action potential due to
who: Absolute refractory period of the neuron

concept.t: During the absolute refractory period, about 1 to 2 milliseconds after a spike, no stimulus of any strength can trigger another action potential.
Voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises.
Next comes the relative refractory period, when only a stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire the cell because the membrane is briefly hyperpolarised.
Refractory periods make action potentials travel one way down the axon and set a ceiling on firing rate.

wrong.2: Here a second spike is possible, but only with a stronger-than-normal stimulus, because the membrane is briefly hyperpolarised.
wrong.3: At rest (about -70 mV) the neuron is ready to fire; firing is not blocked.
wrong.4: Not a technical stage; the active phase is the action potential itself, not the period that follows it.

q: Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: Schertzer and Stone (1974) specified that acceptance requires respect for the individual as a person of warmth. Reason R: Therapists relate to their patients/clients in a non-judgemental, non-critical and non-punitive way. In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: As printed, A says 'warmth' where Bruce Shertzer and Shelley Stone wrote 'worth', probably a copying slip; if the change is deliberate, A is false and (4) is right.
who: Bruce Shertzer and Shelley Stone, Fundamentals of Counseling

concept.t: Bruce Shertzer and Shelley Stone defined acceptance as the counsellor's respect for the client as a person of worth. Reading 'warmth' as a copying slip, A is true.
R is true and explains A: respecting a client's worth is shown by relating in a non-judgemental, non-critical, non-punitive way.
Acceptance is close to Carl Rogers' unconditional positive regard: valuing the client as a person without approving every behaviour.

wrong.2: R is not a separate fact: the non-judgemental, non-critical stance is what respecting a client as a person of worth means, so it does explain A.
wrong.3: R is true; relating without judging, criticising or punishing is the standard description of an accepting counsellor.
wrong.4: Holds only if 'warmth' is a deliberate change; read as 'worth', Shertzer and Stone's definition is true.

q: In Bronfenbrenner's model, which one of the following systems is independent of cultural bias?
doubt: No standard text ranks the systems on cultural bias; the microsystem is chosen as the most immediate, universal setting, with the mesosystem as runner-up for the same reason.
who: Urie Bronfenbrenner, ecological systems theory

concept.t: The microsystem is the child's immediate, face-to-face setting: family, school, peers. Every child in every culture has one, so it is the level least tied to any one culture's values.

Urie Bronfenbrenner placed the child inside nested systems: microsystem, mesosystem (links between microsystems), exosystem (settings that affect the child indirectly), macrosystem (culture) and chronosystem (time).
Culture sits in the macrosystem, the outermost layer, which makes it the most culture-loaded level.

wrong.2: Links between microsystems, such as home and school; how these links work depends on cultural norms like parents' involvement in schooling.
wrong.3: Settings the child is not in, such as a parent's workplace, local government and media, which are shaped by each society's institutions.
wrong.4: The culture itself: its values, laws, customs and ideology, so it is the level least free of cultural bias.

q: Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Efficacy (B) Tolerance (C) Downregulation (D) Withdrawal. List II: (I) Response activated when drugs bind with a receptor (II) Repeated exposure with less activation of receptors (III) Compensatory reduction in receptor availability (IV) Unpleasant physiological responses. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Drug-receptor pharmacology terms

concept.t: (A) Efficacy = (I) response activated when the drug binds the receptor; (B) Tolerance = (II) less receptor activation after repeated exposure; (C) Downregulation = (III) compensatory reduction in receptor availability; (D) Withdrawal = (IV) unpleasant physiological responses.
Affinity is how readily a drug binds a receptor; efficacy is how strongly it activates the receptor once bound.
With repeated use the brain compensates, for example by downregulation (fewer receptors), so the same dose has less effect. Stopping the drug then unmasks these changes as withdrawal.

wrong.1: Swaps A and B: efficacy is the activation produced by binding, while reduced activation after repeated exposure is tolerance.
wrong.3: Wrong throughout: efficacy is not receptor reduction, and withdrawal is the unpleasant aftermath of stopping a drug, not receptor activation.
wrong.4: Wrong throughout: efficacy is activation on binding, downregulation is fewer receptors, and withdrawal is the unpleasant response, not receptor loss.

q: Which one of the following is considered as correct for Poverty Gap?
who: Poverty gap, a measure of poverty depth

concept.t: The poverty gap is the shortfall between the poverty line and the actual income of each person below it, added up or averaged across the population.
If the line is 100 and a person earns 70, the gap is 30. The poverty gap index averages these shortfalls over the whole population (the non-poor count as zero) as a share of the line.
The headcount ratio tells how many people are poor; the poverty gap tells how poor they are.

wrong.1: This is income inequality, measured by tools such as the Gini coefficient, not the poverty gap.
wrong.2: This is the development divide between rich and poor countries, not a measure of individual poverty.
wrong.4: This is an infrastructure or development gap between countries; the poverty gap concerns individual incomes below the poverty line.

q: A harsh father always restricts the curiosity motive of his son and the son develops a general hostility towards his superiors. Which of the following is correct about this?
doubt: The item has no clear textbook source; conditioned, generalised hostility fits best, with (1) the runner-up if the setter used 'represses' loosely to mean 'suppresses'.
who: Classical conditioning and stimulus generalisation

concept.t: The son learned hostility towards the punishing father, and it has spread to other authority figures. That is conditioned hostility carried by stimulus generalisation.

Authority (the father) is repeatedly paired with frustration, so authority itself comes to trigger anger. Superiors resemble the father and trigger the same response, as Little Albert's conditioned fear spread from a rat to other furry objects.
Learned emotional responses can be weakened by extinction or counter-conditioning, so calling such a change permanent goes too far.

wrong.1: Repression in Sigmund Freud's sense is a person's own unconscious defence; the father blocks or punishes the curiosity, he does not repress it.
wrong.2: Learned emotional responses can be reduced by extinction or counter-conditioning, so the change is not necessarily permanent.
wrong.3: A broad attitude learned early and generalised to all superiors is usually resistant to change, not the most modifiable kind of response.

q: Which of the following character strengths are included in the VIA classification of strengths? (A) Creativity (B) Forgiveness (C) Resilience (D) Prudence
who: Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman, VIA classification (2004)

concept.t: The VIA lists 24 character strengths. Creativity falls under wisdom, and forgiveness and prudence under temperance; resilience is not one of the 24.
Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman grouped the 24 strengths under six virtues: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence.
Courage covers bravery, perseverance, honesty and zest. Resilience is studied in positive psychology but is not a VIA strength.

wrong.1: Includes resilience, which is not among the 24 VIA strengths, and leaves out prudence, a temperance strength.
wrong.2: Includes resilience, which the VIA does not list, and leaves out forgiveness, a temperance strength.
wrong.4: Includes resilience, which is not a VIA strength, and omits forgiveness and prudence, which both are.

q: The psychosocial stage of Intimacy v/s Isolation is preceded and succeeded by which of the following? (A) Generativity v/s Stagnation (B) Identity v/s Identity confusion (C) Industry v/s Diffusion
who: Erik Erikson, psychosocial stages (1950)

concept.t: In Erik Erikson's scheme, intimacy vs isolation (stage 6, young adulthood) follows identity vs role confusion (stage 5, adolescence) and precedes generativity vs stagnation (stage 7, middle adulthood).

Trust vs mistrust → autonomy vs shame and doubt → initiative vs guilt → industry vs inferiority → identity vs role confusion → intimacy vs isolation → generativity vs stagnation → integrity vs despair.
A secure identity must come first; only then can a person risk sharing it with another in intimacy.

wrong.1: Gives only the stage that follows; it leaves out identity vs role confusion, the stage just before intimacy.
wrong.2: C is not an Erikson stage: industry pairs with inferiority (stage 4, school age), and 'diffusion' belongs to identity diffusion in stage 5.
wrong.4: Industry (stage 4) is not next to intimacy, and C misprints it as industry vs diffusion; generativity, the following stage, is missing.

q: Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: The obtained t-value will follow the theoretical t-distribution if the underlying assumptions are fulfilled. Reason R: The application of t-test makes an assumption of heterogeneity of variance. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
who: William Gosset ('Student'), t-test assumptions

concept.t: A is true: the computed t follows the theoretical t distribution for its degrees of freedom only when the test's assumptions hold, so its p-values are then accurate.
R is false: the independent t-test assumes homogeneity of variance (equal population variances), not heterogeneity.
The data should come from normal populations and the observations should be independent; Levene's test checks equal variances.
When variances are unequal, use Welch's t-test, which adjusts the degrees of freedom.

wrong.1: R is false: the t-test assumes equal (homogeneous) variances, so it cannot explain A.
wrong.2: R is false, not true: heterogeneity of variance violates the t-test's assumption of equal variances.
wrong.4: A is correct: when normality, independence and equal variances hold, the sampling distribution of t matches the theoretical t distribution.

q: Client: (Silent and shifting nervously in her chair. She is facing the counselor, but her eyes scan anxiously about). Counselor: "It must be difficult for you to decide what you are going to do here with me." This counselor response is an example of:
doubt: The counsellor's line also sounds like a reflection of feeling, so (4) is the runner-up, but it names no feeling and guesses at what lies behind the fidgeting.
who: Responding to client nonverbal behaviour (counselling skills)

concept.t: The counsellor does not name the behaviour or a feeling. Instead the counsellor speculates about the content behind it, that the client is unsure what to do in the session, and responds to that.

A counsellor can respond to nonverbal behaviour by ignoring it, by inviting the client to look at it ('What are you feeling as you shift in your chair?'), or by addressing what seems to be motivating it.
A reflection of feeling names the emotion directly ('You seem anxious'); a speculation adds the counsellor's guess about its cause.
