wrong.2: That would point to the behaviour itself, for example 'I notice you keep looking around the room', and invite the client to talk about it.
wrong.3: That would invite the client to explore her own emotions ('What are you feeling right now?'); here the counsellor offers a guess about the cause instead.
wrong.4: A reflection names the emotion the client shows, such as 'You seem nervous'; this response names no feeling and guesses at its cause.

q: A teacher engages students in hands-on, inquiry-based and relevant learning activities in his class. What does this illustrate? (A) Application of the law of exercise (B) Application of the law of effect (C) Creating intrinsic motivation (D) Creating extrinsic motivation
who: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, intrinsic motivation

concept.t: Hands-on, inquiry-based, relevant tasks make learning interesting in itself, so students work because they want to. That builds intrinsic motivation; no reward or drill is involved.

Intrinsic motivation is doing a task for its own sake: curiosity, interest, challenge. Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory says it grows when learners feel autonomy, competence and relatedness.
Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards such as grades and prizes. Edward Thorndike's laws of exercise and effect are about practice and reward.

wrong.1: Edward Thorndike's law of effect says responses followed by satisfying outcomes are strengthened; the activities here involve no reward, so it does not apply.
wrong.2: C is right, but B, Edward Thorndike's law of effect, depends on rewarding consequences, which the stem does not mention.
wrong.3: C is right, but A, Edward Thorndike's law of exercise, concerns strengthening bonds through repetition and drill, not inquiry or relevance.

q: What do you call the attention that is drawn automatically to a stimulus without the intention of the participant?
who: Michael Posner, exogenous vs endogenous orienting

concept.t: Exogenous attention is captured automatically, bottom-up, by a salient stimulus such as a sudden flash or a loud noise, whatever the person intends.
Endogenous attention is voluntary and top-down: you direct it on purpose, to serve a goal or follow a cue such as an arrow.
In Michael Posner's cueing task, a flash at the target location works fast and automatically; a central arrow works more slowly and needs intention.

wrong.1: This means spreading attention across two or more tasks at once, as in driving while talking; it concerns capacity, not automatic capture.
wrong.2: This is the dichotic listening technique of repeating one ear's message aloud, used by Colin Cherry to study selective attention.
wrong.3: The opposite: voluntary, goal-directed (top-down) attention, which needs the participant's intention.

q: Which one of the following terms denotes that there are qualities of experience that cannot be explained in terms of combinations of traditional kinds of sensations?
who: Christian von Ehrenfels, form qualities (1890)

concept.t: Christian von Ehrenfels coined Gestaltqualitäten (form qualities). A melody stays the same tune in a new key though every note has changed, so the whole is not a sum of sensations.

This challenged the structuralism of Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener, which built experience from elementary sensations. It paved the way for Gestalt psychology (Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Köhler, Kurt Koffka).
Gestalt motto: the whole is different from the sum of its parts.

wrong.1: Means 'spirit of the times', the intellectual climate of an era, a term Edwin Boring used in his history of psychology.
wrong.2: In Jacques Loeb's work, an automatic, forced orientation of an organism towards or away from a stimulus such as light.
wrong.4: The old name for the pineal gland, which René Descartes saw as the point where mind and body interact.

q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is released by which of the following?
who: Hypothalamus and posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)

concept.t: ADH (vasopressin) is made by neurons in the hypothalamus, travels down their axons and is released into the blood from the posterior pituitary.
ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb water, so less urine is produced. It is released when the body is dehydrated or blood volume falls.
The posterior pituitary releases only two hormones, ADH and oxytocin; the anterior pituitary makes its own hormones (GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin).

wrong.1: Secretes corticosteroids: cortisol (a glucocorticoid), aldosterone (a mineralocorticoid) and adrenal sex hormones.
wrong.2: Releases adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline during the fight-or-flight response.
wrong.3: Makes and releases its own hormones, such as growth hormone, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH and prolactin, under control of hypothalamic releasing hormones.

q: Which of the following dimensions are essential to be mastered in multicultural counseling, as per McFadden's transcultural perspective? (A) Cultural-Historical (B) Historical hostility management (C) Scientific-Ideological (D) Minority identity management (E) Social
who: John McFadden, stylistic model of transcultural counselling

concept.t: John McFadden's transcultural model says counsellors must master three dimensions: cultural-historical, psychosocial and scientific-ideological. 'Social' in (E) stands for the psychosocial dimension.

Cultural-historical: knowing the client's culture and its history. Psychosocial: how the group's social and psychological patterns shape the client; scientific-ideological: choosing counselling approaches that fit those realities.
McFadden = three dimensions, C-P-S: cultural-historical, psychosocial, scientific-ideological.

wrong.1: Historical hostility management is not one of McFadden's three dimensions, and this set leaves out the scientific-ideological dimension.
wrong.2: Neither historical hostility management nor minority identity management is a McFadden dimension; psychosocial and scientific-ideological are missing.
wrong.3: Only (E) is a McFadden dimension; historical hostility and minority identity management are not, and cultural-historical and scientific-ideological are missing.

q: Which one of the following models proposes that there are three major functional units of the brain: focussing on sustaining attention; receiving and storing information; and planning and self-monitoring?
who: J. P. Das, Jack Naglieri, John Kirby, after Alexander Luria

concept.t: The PASS model (Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, Successive) of J. P. Das, Jack Naglieri and John Kirby is built on Alexander Luria's three functional units of the brain.

Unit 1 (brainstem, reticular system): arousal and attention. Unit 2 (occipital, parietal, temporal lobes): receiving, coding and storing information; Unit 3 (frontal lobes): planning and self-monitoring.
The Cognitive Assessment System (CAS) by Jack Naglieri and J. P. Das measures the four PASS processes.

wrong.2: Kar and Parrila co-wrote on cognitive planning with J. P. Das, but the three functional units framework is Luria's, formalised as the PASS model.
wrong.3: Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin's multi-store model describes memory stores (sensory, short-term, long-term), not functional units of the brain.
wrong.4: Earl Hunt studied intelligence through speed of information processing (the cognitive correlates approach), not Luria's three brain units.

q: Which of the following are the components of Metacognition? (A) Metacognitive knowledge (B) Metacognitive experience (C) Metacognitive control (D) Metacognitive regulation
doubt: Control and regulation are near synonyms (Thomas Nelson and Louis Narens speak of monitoring and control), so (3) is the runner-up; most texts use the term regulation.
who: John Flavell (1979); Ann Brown, metacognitive regulation

concept.t: Metacognition is usually split into three parts: metacognitive knowledge (what you know about thinking), metacognitive experiences (feelings during a task, such as 'I don't get this') and metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating).
John Flavell introduced metacognition, 'thinking about thinking', with knowledge and experiences. Ann Brown stressed the regulation of cognition.
Regulation and control mean much the same; when both appear, regulation is the standard textbook label.

wrong.1: Knowledge and experiences are John Flavell's two parts, but this leaves out metacognitive regulation, the planning and monitoring side.
wrong.2: Knowledge and regulation is the two-part split used by Ann Brown, but it omits metacognitive experiences, the third standard component.
wrong.3: Control is close in meaning to regulation, but the standard three-part list names the third component metacognitive regulation.

q: Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: Many companies now enable their employees to share profits or even to participate in company ownership. Reason R: Workers' productivity boosts rewards from employers. In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
doubt: R can be read as reversing cause and effect (rewards are meant to boost productivity), in which case (2) is the runner-up.
who: Profit-sharing and employee ownership, pay for performance

concept.t: A is true: many firms run profit-sharing and employee share ownership schemes, so workers gain when the company does well.
R is true and explains A: under these schemes, higher worker productivity raises profits, which raises workers' rewards, so pay is tied to performance.
Linking rewards to results acts as positive reinforcement and gives workers a sense of ownership, which motivates effort.

wrong.2: R is not unrelated: profit-sharing exists precisely so that higher productivity turns into higher rewards, which is why firms offer it.
wrong.3: R is true; in pay-for-performance schemes such as profit-sharing and gainsharing, higher productivity does raise what employees receive.
wrong.4: A is true; profit-sharing plans and employee share ownership plans are common in modern companies.

q: Who among the following conducted one of the most famous and controversial experiments in the area of obedience?
who: Stanley Milgram, obedience studies at Yale (1963)

concept.t: Stanley Milgram had participants, as 'teachers', give what they thought were rising electric shocks to a 'learner'. About 65 percent went to the maximum 450 volts when the experimenter insisted.
The learner was an actor and no shocks were real, but participants were deceived and suffered real stress. This drove later ethics rules on deception and debriefing.
Obedience = following orders from an authority; conformity (Solomon Asch) = going along with peers; compliance (Robert Cialdini) = yielding to a direct request.

wrong.1: Muzafer Sherif studied norm formation with the autokinetic effect and intergroup conflict in the Robbers Cave study, not obedience.
wrong.2: Solomon Asch studied conformity: people agreeing with a group's obviously wrong judgements of line length.
wrong.4: Robert Cialdini studies influence and compliance tactics such as reciprocity and commitment, not obedience to authority.

q: Teplov, while discussing strong/weak nervous systems, believed that the point of 'transmarginal inhibition' is the point beyond which:
doubt: The options look garbled: the real idea is that response falls as intensity rises, which (2) states in reverse, while (1) would be right if its second 'decreases' was meant to be 'increases'.
who: Boris Teplov, after Ivan Pavlov's law of strength

concept.t: Below the threshold of transmarginal inhibition, response grows with stimulus intensity. Beyond it the relation reverses: stronger stimuli give weaker responses, so lowering intensity makes the response rise, as (2) says.
Ivan Pavlov saw transmarginal (protective) inhibition as the nervous system shielding itself from overload. Boris Teplov measured strength of the nervous system by how high this threshold lies.
A strong nervous system tolerates intense stimulation before inhibition sets in; a weak one is more sensitive and reaches the point sooner.

wrong.1: Below the threshold, response falls when intensity falls; that is the ordinary law of strength, not what happens beyond transmarginal inhibition.
wrong.3: Beyond the threshold, response still depends on intensity, but inversely; it does not keep rising whatever the stimulus does.
wrong.4: Response does not fall whatever happens: beyond the threshold it falls when intensity rises but recovers when intensity is lowered.

q: Which of the following were considered to be appropriate for psychological study by Wundt? (A) Analysis of cultural products (B) Higher mental processes (C) The totality of psychological phenomena (D) Self-observation (E) Physiological type of experimentation
doubt: Wundt did study higher mental processes (B), but only indirectly through cultural products, so the item is loosely worded; if 'totality of phenomena' (C) is counted as wrong, the answer becomes (3).
who: Wilhelm Wundt, experimental psychology and Völkerpsychologie

concept.t: Wilhelm Wundt defined psychology as the study of the whole content of immediate experience (C). He studied it by controlled self-observation (D) using the experimental method of physiology (E).

For complex processes such as language, thought and morals, Wundt said lab experiments were unsuitable. He studied them through cultural products like language, myth and custom (A) in his ten-volume Völkerpsychologie (folk psychology).
That is the trap: Wundt held that higher mental processes could not be studied directly by experiment; only their cultural products could be analysed.
Wundt = trained introspection plus the physiological method for simple processes; Völkerpsychologie for complex social and cultural ones.

wrong.1: Leaves out cultural products (A) and physiological experimentation (E), both central to Wundt, and includes higher mental processes, which he kept out of experimental study.
wrong.2: Includes higher mental processes (B), which Wundt kept out of the laboratory, and drops the analysis of cultural products (A), the core of his Völkerpsychologie.
wrong.3: Rightly keeps A, D and E but drops C; Wundt defined psychology as the study of the whole content of immediate experience.

q: Match List I with List II. List I: (A) Aggression (B) Anti-Social Aggression (C) Prosocial Aggression (D) Sanctioned Aggression. List II: (I) Aggression that is permissible according to the norms of the individual's social group (II) Aggressive acts that support commonly accepted social norms (III) Any action intended to hurt another person (IV) Aggressive acts that violate commonly accepted social norms. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Shelley Taylor, Letitia Peplau, David Sears: kinds of aggression

concept.t: (A) Aggression = (III) any action intended to hurt another person; (B) Anti-social aggression = (IV) acts that violate accepted social norms; (C) Prosocial aggression = (II) acts that support accepted norms; (D) Sanctioned aggression = (I) acts the group's norms permit.

The test is the social norm. Anti-social aggression breaks it (a mugging); prosocial aggression enforces it (police stopping a gunman); sanctioned aggression is not required but allowed (hitting an attacker in self-defence).
The general definition of aggression rests on the intent to harm, not on whether harm actually happens.

wrong.1: Gives the general definition (III) to prosocial aggression and the norm-breaking meaning (IV) to aggression in general; prosocial aggression is the kind that supports norms.
wrong.3: Every pair is wrong: anti-social aggression violates norms (IV) rather than supporting them, and sanctioned aggression is what group norms permit (I).
wrong.4: Every pair is wrong: aggression in general is any act meant to hurt (III), and prosocial aggression is the kind that supports norms (II).

q: Arrange the pairings of US and CS in classical conditioning in terms of onset of US in relation to CS, starting from the earliest. (A) Backward (B) Simultaneous (C) Delayed (D) Trace
who: Pavlovian conditioning: CS-US timing procedures

concept.t: Backward (US comes before the CS) → Simultaneous (US starts with the CS) → Delayed (US starts while the CS is still on) → Trace (US starts only after the CS has ended).
The conditioned stimulus (CS) is the signal and the unconditioned stimulus (US) is the event it predicts. Moving from backward to trace, the US arrives later and later relative to CS onset.
Delayed conditioning usually gives the strongest learning; trace weakens as the gap grows; backward conditioning is the weakest and often produces inhibition.

wrong.2: Puts trace first, but in trace conditioning the US arrives only after the CS has ended, so its onset is the latest, not the earliest.
wrong.3: Starts with delayed and ends with backward, nearly reversing the order; backward is the only procedure in which the US comes before the CS.
wrong.4: Places trace and delayed ahead of backward and simultaneous, when those two have the earliest US onset.

q: The Door in the Face Technique is based on which tactic of compliance?
who: Robert Cialdini, door-in-the-face technique

concept.t: In the door-in-the-face technique a large request is refused, then the asker retreats to a smaller one. The retreat looks like a concession, and the norm of reciprocity pushes the target to concede in return by agreeing.

Robert Cialdini's team asked students to counsel young offenders two hours a week for two years (refused), then to take them on a two-hour zoo trip; far more agreed than when asked for the zoo trip alone.
Robert Baron and Donn Byrne group door-in-the-face and that's-not-all under reciprocity; foot-in-the-door and lowball fall under commitment or consistency.

wrong.2: This group covers foot-in-the-door and lowball, which build on an earlier small yes, not on a refused large request.
wrong.3: This group covers ingratiation, flattery and self-presentation, which work by making the target like the requester.
wrong.4: This group covers playing hard to get and the deadline technique, which make an offer seem rare or short-lived.

q: Cognitive theory contends that dependency behaviours arise from and are maintained by cognitive distortions and maladaptive thought processes. Which of the following are associated with cognitive distortions? (A) Availability (B) Hindsight bias (C) Flexible attribution (D) Illusion of control
who: Cognitive model of gambling and other dependencies

concept.t: All four are recognised cognitive distortions in problem gambling and other dependencies. Each keeps the person believing that carrying on will pay off.
Availability: vivid, easily recalled wins seem more common than they are. Hindsight bias: after an outcome the person feels it was predictable, so they trust their future predictions.
Flexible attribution: wins are credited to skill, losses blamed on bad luck or near misses. Illusion of control (Ellen Langer): belief that one can influence chance outcomes.
Add the gambler's fallacy (a win is 'due' after a run of losses) to the same list.

wrong.2: Leaves out illusion of control, the best known gambling distortion, in which a person believes skill or rituals can sway chance outcomes.
wrong.3: Leaves out availability: vividly remembered wins feel more frequent than they are, which feeds continued gambling or use.
wrong.4: Leaves out availability and hindsight bias, both standard distortions that make wins seem common and outcomes seem predictable.

q: What does 'Absolute Poverty' mean?
who: Indian poverty line, minimum calorie norm

concept.t: Absolute poverty means income too low to meet basic needs. In India it has been measured by the money needed for a minimum calorie intake: 2,400 kcal per person per day in rural areas and 2,100 in urban areas.
Relative poverty compares a person's income with others in the same society; absolute poverty uses a fixed minimum standard, however others live.
The poverty line is the money value of that minimum consumption basket; people below it are counted as absolutely poor.

wrong.1: The number of poor people is the headcount, a way of counting poverty, not its meaning; absolute poverty refers to a fixed minimum standard of living.
wrong.2: Prices are used to turn the minimum consumption basket into a money poverty line, but absolute poverty itself is defined by the minimum needs.
wrong.3: Unemployment is a cause and correlate of poverty, not the definition of absolute poverty.

q: In cognitive therapy by Ellis, arrange the sequence of the following after recognising the activating event. (A) Discriminating the new emotional/behavioural consequences (B) Recognising the emotional/behavioural consequences of belief (C) Understanding the corresponding beliefs (D) Challenging and counteracting these beliefs (E) Recognising new feelings
doubt: Read by the letters of the ABC model, the belief comes before the consequence, which gives C-B-D-A-E, option (2), the runner-up.
who: Albert Ellis, REBT ABCDE model

concept.t: After the activating event: recognise the emotional and behavioural consequences (B), find the beliefs behind them (C), dispute the beliefs (D), discriminate the new consequences (A), recognise new feelings (E). So B-C-D-A-E.
The client arrives with the upsetting feeling, so the therapist assesses the consequence first and then looks for the corresponding irrational belief that produced it.
Albert Ellis held that events do not upset us directly; our irrational beliefs about them do. Disputing those beliefs produces a more effective outlook and healthier feelings.
ABCDEF = Activating event, Belief, Consequence, Disputing, Effect (new effective philosophy), new Feelings, as set out by Gerald Corey.

wrong.1: Starts right with consequences then beliefs, but leaves disputing to the end, when disputing must come before any new consequences or feelings appear.
wrong.2: Puts the belief first, the literal letter order of ABC; in practice the therapist starts from the upsetting consequence and then finds the corresponding belief.
wrong.3: Puts the belief first and places the new consequences and feelings before disputing, when they are the result of disputing.

q: Match List I with List II. List I (Sources of Personal Efficacy by Bandura): (A) Performance accomplishment (B) Vicarious experiences (C) Verbal persuasion (D) Emotional arousal. List II (Therapeutic processes): (I) Live models, symbolic modelling (II) Attribution, relaxation biofeedback, symbolic desensitisation (III) Participant modelling, performance exposure (IV) Suggestion, exhortation, self-instruction. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Albert Bandura, self-efficacy theory (1977)

concept.t: (A) Performance accomplishment = (III) participant modelling, performance exposure; (B) Vicarious experience = (I) live and symbolic modelling; (C) Verbal persuasion = (IV) suggestion, exhortation, self-instruction; (D) Emotional arousal = (II) attribution, relaxation biofeedback, symbolic desensitisation.
Self-efficacy is the belief that one can carry out a behaviour. Albert Bandura named four sources of it, and each therapy raises efficacy through one of them.
Performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) are the strongest source, because they rest on one's own success.

wrong.1: Gives vicarious experience the arousal methods (II) and emotional arousal the modelling methods (I); watching models is the vicarious source.
wrong.2: Swaps the first two sources: participant modelling is a performance method, while live and symbolic modelling are vicarious; it also swaps persuasion and arousal.
wrong.3: Every pair is wrong: relaxation and biofeedback lower emotional arousal, live models are vicarious, and suggestion and exhortation are verbal persuasion.

q: Who believed that meaning in life can be uncovered by creative, experiential and attitudinal values?
who: Viktor Frankl, logotherapy

concept.t: Viktor Frankl said meaning is found three ways: creative values (what we give the world through work or deeds), experiential values (what we take from it, such as love or beauty) and attitudinal values (the stand we take toward unavoidable suffering).
Frankl, a concentration camp survivor, founded logotherapy and saw the will to meaning as the main human motive (Man's Search for Meaning).
Attitudinal values remain even when nothing can be changed: a person can still choose their attitude to suffering.

wrong.1: American existential psychologist who wrote on anxiety, love and will and the courage to create, not on the three value routes to meaning.
wrong.3: German philosopher of the will to power and the Übermensch; Frankl quoted his line that one who has a why to live can bear almost any how.
wrong.4: French existentialist who held that existence precedes essence and that we create meaning through free choice, not through three types of value.

q: Which of the following is an attitude measure that places a single adjective in the centre of an even number of numerical values?
who: Jan Stapel, unipolar rating scale

concept.t: The Stapel scale puts one adjective (say 'Friendly') in the middle of a column of numbers, usually +5 to -5 with no zero. The respondent picks how well the word describes the object.
It is a one-pole version of the semantic differential, so there is no need to find an exact opposite adjective for each item.
Stapel = single adjective, even number of points (10). Semantic differential = two bipolar adjectives at the ends of a usually seven-point line.

wrong.1: Allen Edwards is known for the scale discrimination technique, which blends Thurstone and Likert methods, and for work on social desirability; no central adjective is used.
wrong.2: Louis Thurstone's method of equal-appearing intervals has judges rate statements on an 11-point scale; respondents then endorse statements of known scale value.
wrong.4: Charles Osgood's tool places the object between two opposite adjectives (good to bad) on a usually seven-point scale, not one adjective in the centre.

q: Total cholesterol is determined by adding which of the following values?
who: Friedewald formula: VLDL cholesterol = triglycerides ÷ 5

concept.t: Total cholesterol is the cholesterol carried in HDL, LDL and VLDL. VLDL cholesterol is estimated as triglycerides ÷ 5, that is 20% of triglycerides (in mg/dL).
Labs use the same relation rearranged, the Friedewald formula: LDL = total cholesterol - HDL - (triglycerides ÷ 5).
High LDL ('bad') raises the risk of coronary heart disease; high HDL ('good') protects against it.

wrong.1: Leaves out VLDL cholesterol, which carries part of the blood's cholesterol, so this sum would underestimate the total.
wrong.2: VLDL counts in full, not as 30%; the one-fifth rule applies to triglycerides, which are used to estimate VLDL.
wrong.3: Same error: the whole VLDL value counts; only triglycerides are scaled, by one fifth, to estimate it.

q: What is the correct sequence of transformation in integral yoga? (A) Transformation of physical (B) Transformation of subconscient (C) Transformation of mind (D) Transformation of vital (E) Transformation of inconscient
who: Sri Aurobindo, Integral Yoga

concept.t: Mind (C) → vital (D) → physical (A) → subconscient (B) → inconscient (E).

In Sri Aurobindo's Integral Yoga the higher consciousness descends from above, so the parts of the being change from the top down: first the mind, then the vital (life force, desires, emotions), then the body, and lastly the hidden subconscient and inconscient bases.
The deeper the level, the later and harder its change; the inconscient is the last and most resistant.

wrong.2: Starts with the physical, but in Integral Yoga the body is among the last parts to change; the descent begins with the mind.
wrong.3: Reverses mind, vital and physical, working upward from the body, whereas Aurobindo's transformation works downward from the mind.
wrong.4: Puts the physical before the vital, but the vital (desires and emotions) lies between mind and body and is transformed before the body.

q: What comprises haptic perception? (A) Shape (B) Size (C) Volume (D) Identity
doubt: Volume can also be judged by enclosing an object in the hand, so (1) is defensible; the item seems to follow a definition listing shape, size and identity.
who: James J. Gibson, active touch; Susan Lederman and Roberta Klatzky

concept.t: Haptic perception is perception by active touch: the hand moves over an object. It gives the object's shape and size and lets us recognise what it is (its identity), often within a couple of seconds without looking.

Hand movements combine skin input with kinaesthetic information from muscles and joints. Susan Lederman and Roberta Klatzky described exploratory procedures: contour following for shape, lateral motion for texture, pressure for hardness.
Tactile (passive) perception = touch applied to a still hand; haptic = active exploration, the distinction drawn by James J. Gibson.

wrong.1: Drops identity, yet recognising what an object is by touch alone (haptic object recognition) is a main function of haptic perception.
wrong.2: Drops size, which active touch judges directly, for example from how far the fingers spread around an object.
wrong.3: Drops shape, the property most clearly given by haptic exploration, especially by tracing an object's contours with the fingers.

q: Which neurotransmitter is helpful in synaptic plasticity?
who: Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo, long-term potentiation

concept.t: Glutamate, the brain's main excitatory transmitter, drives long-term potentiation (LTP), the best studied form of synaptic plasticity, especially in the hippocampus.
When the cell is depolarised enough to remove the magnesium block, glutamate opens NMDA receptors. Calcium flows in and triggers changes, such as extra AMPA receptors, that strengthen the synapse.
The NMDA receptor is a coincidence detector (it needs glutamate and depolarisation together), a cellular version of Donald Hebb's rule.

wrong.1: The transmitter at the neuromuscular junction and in attention and memory circuits (lost in Alzheimer's disease); LTP itself depends mainly on glutamate.
wrong.3: The main inhibitory transmitter; it opposes the depolarisation that NMDA-dependent plasticity needs.
wrong.4: Signals reward and prediction error and can modulate plasticity, but it does not directly induce LTP.

q: What is the correct sequence of the Decision Making Perspective of Pro-social behaviour to help a person in distress? (A) Taking personal responsibility (B) Weighing the cost and benefits (C) Perceiving a need (D) Deciding how to help
who: Shelley Taylor, Letitia Peplau, David Sears: decision model of helping

concept.t: Perceiving a need (C) → taking personal responsibility (A) → weighing costs and benefits (B) → deciding how to help (D), then acting.

A bystander must first notice the event and interpret it as an emergency, then feel personally responsible, then judge whether the rewards of helping outweigh the costs, and only then choose what to do.
Diffusion of responsibility blocks the second step: the more bystanders, the less each feels responsible (Bibb Latané and John Darley's bystander studies).

wrong.1: Puts responsibility before noticing the need; no one can take responsibility for a problem they have not yet perceived.
wrong.2: Starts by weighing costs and benefits, which comes only after the need is perceived and responsibility accepted.
wrong.3: Puts taking responsibility first and perceiving the need third; the model begins with noticing and interpreting the situation.

q:
Comprehension (Q91-Q95): A researcher wanted to predict academic achievement using Intelligence Test-A (IT-A), Intelligence Test-B (IT-B), Type of school (rural/urban), and conscientiousness as predictors, using multiple regression analysis on data from 200 students. The OLS estimator was used. For the entire model F = 8.9, p < .01. In individual predictor analysis, IT-B was the insignificant predictor. A suitable test indicated homoscedasticity. The model R² = 0.64 and adjusted R² = 0.59. Both intelligence tests are significantly correlated with the criterion variable and with each other. 
 What is indicated by R² in the passage?
who: Coefficient of determination (R²)

concept.t: R², the coefficient of determination, is the share of criterion variance explained by all predictors together. R² = 0.64, so 0.64 × 100 = 64% of the variance in academic achievement is explained.
Adjusted R² (0.59) corrects for the number of predictors and sample size, so it is slightly smaller; 59% is the better estimate for the population.
Unexplained variance = 1 - R² = 0.36 (36%). The multiple correlation R = √0.64 = 0.80.

wrong.2: This is the multiple correlation R (√0.64 = 0.80) read as a percentage; variance explained uses the squared value, R².
wrong.3: Half of R²; nothing in the conversion halves R², which reads directly as 64%.
wrong.4: This is 1 - R², the share of variance the predictors leave unexplained.

q: Which of the following is correct about the residual variance in the passage?
who: OLS regression assumptions, homoscedastic residuals

concept.t: The test showed homoscedasticity: residuals spread equally at every level of the predicted score. With the OLS assumptions met, residuals are randomly distributed around zero with no pattern.
A residual is observed minus predicted score (Y - Ŷ). OLS picks the weights that make the sum of squared residuals smallest, and by construction leaves residuals uncorrelated with the predictors.
A funnel or curve in the residual plot signals heteroscedasticity or non-linearity, that is, systematic error.

wrong.1: OLS residuals are uncorrelated with every predictor by construction; any such correlation would mean the model had missed predictable variance.
wrong.2: Residuals are part of the criterion score, so some overlap with it is built in; the assumption that matters is that they show no systematic pattern.
wrong.3: A systematic pattern, such as a funnel or curve, would signal heteroscedasticity or a mis-specified model, the opposite of what the test found.

q: What kind of a variable is 'type of school' in the passage?
who: Dummy coding of categorical predictors

concept.t: Type of school has two categories (rural, urban). To enter it in a regression it is coded 0 and 1 (rural = 0, urban = 1), which makes it a dummy variable.
The weight of a dummy variable is the difference in predicted achievement between urban and rural students, other predictors held constant. A variable with k categories needs k - 1 dummies.
A moderator changes the strength of an X-Y link (tested with an interaction term); a mediator carries the effect from X to Y. The passage tests neither.

wrong.1: That role changes the strength or direction of a predictor-criterion link and is tested with an interaction term; school type here is simply one more predictor.
wrong.2: That role lies on the causal path from predictor to criterion (X → M → Y); the passage does not model school type that way.
wrong.4: That label fits variables with many ordered values, like rating scale totals; rural/urban has just two unordered categories.

q: Which of the following is the reason for the insignificance of IT-B?
who: Multicollinearity in multiple regression

concept.t: IT-B correlates with achievement but also with IT-A. Once IT-A is in the model, IT-B adds little unique variance and its standard error inflates, so its weight is not significant. This is multicollinearity.
Regression weights reflect each predictor's unique contribution. When two predictors overlap, the variance they share is not credited to either one.
Check it with the variance inflation factor (VIF) or tolerance; VIF above 10 (tolerance below 0.1) is a common warning sign.

wrong.1: Ruled out: the passage says a suitable test showed homoscedasticity.
wrong.2: IT-B is significantly correlated with achievement, so on its own it does predict; it loses significance only because its variance overlaps with IT-A.
wrong.3: 200 students for four predictors is ample, and the other predictors reached significance in the same sample.

q: Which of the following is the df for F for the entire model?
who: F-test degrees of freedom in regression

concept.t: For the whole model, df1 (regression) = k = number of predictors = 4, and df2 (residual) = N - k - 1 = 200 - 4 - 1 = 195.
F = mean square regression ÷ mean square residual, each mean square being its sum of squares divided by its df. Total df = N - 1 = 199 = 4 + 195.
The extra 1 subtracted in the residual df is for the intercept.

wrong.2: 199 is the total df (N - 1); the residual df must also lose one df for each of the four predictors.
wrong.3: There are four predictors (IT-A, IT-B, school type, conscientiousness), not three, so df<sub>1</sub> = 4 and df<sub>2</sub> = 195.
wrong.4: Uses three predictors and the total df; the model has four predictors, and the residual df is 195.

q:
Comprehension (Q96-Q100): A psychologist developed a scale measuring warmth and competence dimensions. She factor-analysed 25 items to retain 20 items, choosing Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). Bartlett's test = 237.8, p < .001. The overall Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure was 0.89. Principal Components Analysis (PCA) was used to extract components. The first eight eigenvalues were 9.9, 6.5, 1.6, 1.00, 0.85, 0.83, 0.82 and 0.79. Factors were retained on the basis of the scree plot and rotated using the varimax criterion. Three items showed cross-loadings, eighteen items loaded on only one factor, and the remaining items did not load on any factor. 
 The Bartlett's test results in the above study suggested that:
who: Bartlett's test of sphericity

concept.t: Bartlett's test of sphericity tests the null hypothesis that the population correlation matrix is an identity matrix. Here the value is 237.8, p < .001, so the null is rejected: the items do correlate in the population.
An identity matrix has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, meaning no item correlates with any other. Then there would be no common factors to extract.
A significant Bartlett test plus KMO above 0.6 (here 0.89) shows the data suit factor analysis.

wrong.2: This is the null hypothesis, which the significant result (p < .001) rejects; only a non-significant test would point to an identity matrix.
wrong.3: Significance tests make inferences about the population; the sample matrix is observed directly and is almost never exactly an identity matrix.
wrong.4: The test concerns the population, not the sample, and the significant result points away from an identity matrix, not towards one.

q: Which of the following is correct for the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin test? (A) It is a test of sampling adequacy (B) Chi-square test is used to test the significance (C) Values smaller than 0.5 are desirable (D) Smaller partial correlation leads to high KMO
who: Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy

concept.t: A is true: KMO is a measure of sampling adequacy. D is true: KMO compares simple correlations with partial correlations, so small partials give a high KMO.
B: KMO is an index from 0 to 1 with no chi-square test; chi-square belongs to Bartlett's test. C: values below 0.5 are unacceptable; higher is better.
KMO = Σr² ÷ (Σr² + Σpartial r²). When items share common factors, partial correlations are small and KMO nears 1. The passage's 0.89 is 'meritorious' on Henry Kaiser's labels.

wrong.1: A is true but incomplete: D is also true, because KMO rises as partial correlations shrink relative to simple correlations.
wrong.2: B is false: KMO is a descriptive index from 0 to 1; the chi-square significance test belongs to Bartlett's test of sphericity.
wrong.4: B and C are false: KMO has no chi-square test, and values below 0.5 make the data unacceptable for factor analysis; it also omits the true statement A.

q: Which of the following is correct in case of the three items having cross-loading?
who: Louis Thurstone, simple structure

concept.t: A cross-loading item loads substantially on two or more factors, so it does not measure one dimension cleanly. In scale building such items are usually dropped.
Louis Thurstone's simple structure asks that each item load highly on one factor and near zero on the rest; varimax rotation aims at this.
Items that load on no factor, like the remaining items in the passage, are also deleted.

wrong.1: Cross-loading weakens construct validity, because the item does not clearly belong to warmth or to competence.
wrong.2: An item that loads on two dimensions is conceptually ambiguous, not sound; its wording probably taps both constructs.
wrong.3: Cross-loading is a problem of factorial validity for three items; by itself it says nothing about the reliability of the whole scale.

q: In the above example, what percentage of the variance would be explained by the first unrotated factor?
who: Variance explained = eigenvalue ÷ number of variables

concept.t: In PCA each standardised item contributes 1 unit of variance, so total variance = number of items analysed = 25. Variance explained = eigenvalue ÷ items × 100 = 9.9 ÷ 25 × 100 = 39.6%.
An eigenvalue is the sum of squared loadings of all items on a component, that is, how much of the total variance it captures.
Rotation (varimax) redistributes variance among the retained factors, which is why the question asks about the unrotated factor.

wrong.1: This is the eigenvalue itself, not a percentage; it must be divided by the 25 items to give the share of total variance.
wrong.3: This is the cumulative variance of the first two components: (9.9 + 6.5) ÷ 25 = 16.4 ÷ 25 = 65.6%.
wrong.4: This is the cumulative variance of the first three components: (9.9 + 6.5 + 1.6) ÷ 25 = 18 ÷ 25 = 72%.

q: Using the Kaiser-Guttman criterion, how many factors would be retained in the above study?
who: Louis Guttman and Henry Kaiser, eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule

concept.t: The Kaiser-Guttman criterion keeps components with eigenvalues greater than 1. Only 9.9, 6.5 and 1.6 exceed 1, so 3 factors are kept; the fourth value, 1.00, is not greater than 1.
A component with an eigenvalue below 1 explains less variance than a single standardised item, so it is not worth keeping.
The rule often keeps too many factors; the scree plot (Raymond Cattell) and parallel analysis are better guides. Here the sharp drop after 6.5 points to two factors, warmth and competence.

wrong.1: Counts the eigenvalue of exactly 1.00, but the criterion keeps only values greater than 1, so the fourth component is dropped.
wrong.2: This is just the number of eigenvalues reported; four of them are below 1 and one is exactly 1.
wrong.3: This is what the scree plot suggests (the elbow after 6.5) and fits the two-dimension theory, but the Kaiser-Guttman count is 3.
